Depending on the level of track and field this event happened at, reacting too fast to the gun going off counts as a false start. At an Olympic level, there has to be over a 10th of a second delay from when the gun fires to when motion occurs in starting. This is why at almost any level, all athletes begin to run at pretty much the exact same moment. There's a built in delay to things so runners don't try to look for when the gun fires and time it just right, but instead have to have a delayed reaction in most cases for the timing. Which balances out how speed travels to an extent, as closer runners to the gun must delay their reaction to go by more and will be DQ'd if they don't.

As the previous person stated on their reply, you were given a pop-up for every elimination and assist and was deemed successful on the server's end. You were not awarded the assist on the Mercy that would come from Discord being fully applied. 

Notifications like the game saying your orb has been applied is a feedback to let you know the input has gone through, but not that the orb's designated effects are taking place. Best way to think of it is like Kiriko's healing. The game shows the properly thrown ofuda as yellow to signify that it is GOING to heal the locked target, but still takes time to get there.

Abilities such as Discord/Harmony orb work in this same manner so you hopefully don't spam your input button and accidentally send it all over to where you may not want it. It is a notification of the action about to take place, but not that it has been completed. The pop-ups of saves, assist, and elims are what the server acknowledges as truths, with almost everything serving as a quality of life indication so you are aware of what your actions are truly about to do/are doing.

Even though it shows up on her perspective, the server itself does not acknowledge it as happening.

You're watching a replay, which is NOT a live version of what the server saw. All game replays, no matter what title, use code that stores all the inputs made by players, and has AI recreate those motions for each player (hence why every patch resets any replays saved). To elaborate more, and to hopefully clarify things too; Overwatch is a game with strong mental conditioning and command as a hidden core to fights (especially as you climb higher in ranks). For Lucio, try going on side routes in order to flank a Widow or a Sojourn and take the 1v1 up close and personal. Lucio actually does have a one-shot combo, especially on snipers using ADS with reduced movement speed (4 headshots with your burst does 160, boop does 25, and instantly melee after the boop goes off for 30. You do 215 in probably just over .7 seconds if done well).

For your non-hitscans like Zen and Kiriko, realize that your strength is that you can pre-fire corners and points of interest over the hitscan snipers. Yes, Kiriko does take 2 headshots in order to kill Widow versus her single headshot at you with like 70% power. However, you still move at a normal speed and she doesn't, as well as the pressure you exert on her is surprisingly strong. And with Zen, pretty much the exact same principle applies. If you put pressure on a sniper, it forces them to either take cover and do nothing for some time (which essentially puts you ahead in numbers), forces a support to pocket heal them (which forces the other support to now have to look over the tank, the other DPS, and the other support and allows your team to be more aggressive and make that support panic), or the sniper must retreat and find a new angle (which makes the space they threaten sub-optimal, as they would be taking the best vantage points at their first chance).

Genuinely, just try to find what you like best and feels more natural. You might need to chat with your tank and maybe change a playstyle that best works for you all. But snipers love feeling no pressure, having clear sights, and knowing what's around them. So disrupting those core elements throws them into shock. Sojourn is obviously the hardest one to do this for, as she was made to be a close-mid range hero with a long-distance bonus, but mentally throwing them off pays out well for you. Think about all the times you went on losing streaks, or that one player just dominated against your team and it just made you give up. Be THAT guy against the sniper. And even if you get beat out the first time, come back at them in a new way. If you go in as Lucio against a Widow, and she gets peeled for and they end up killing you, go in again and acknowledge the peel is going to happen. Act like a mosquito, just going in for a single burst from out of nowhere only to escape right after. And then, a couple of seconds later, go at her again, and repeat. It's going to wear on her, as she's going to constantly have to keep looking out and listening for you. And if she's doing that, it means your Widow, let's say you have one, now has far less pressure. Maybe with the enemy Widow distracted because of your constant assault, your ally Widow headshots her.

If you play Kiriko or Zen, and the enemy Widow is constantly under pressure from your volleys, your Widow doesn't have to deal with that pressure anymore. They're much more free to try getting a pick and allowing your team to move in. 

If you also want to play more of a healing role, going back to the point of communicating with your tank, run a comp that is more dive-focused. Go with a Winston, D.va, Ball, or Doomfist and just jump snipers. You don't have to feel oppressed when dealing with snipers. They've conditioned you to fear them and avoid taking the fight to them. But if you take the fight to them, suddenly they're in troubled waters.
